title: Maximum Sum Queries
description: Brute force to optimized: offline sorting by one threshold dimension, swept with a monotonic stack keyed by the other, answered via binary search.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2 of equal length n (0-indexed), and a 2D array queries where queries[i] = [x_i, y_i], for each query find the maximum value of nums1[j] + nums2[j] among all indices j such that nums1[j] >= x_i AND nums2[j] >= y_i. If no such index exists for a query, the answer for it is -1.

blocks.text: Each query asks: among all indices where nums1 is at least x AND nums2 is at least y, what is the largest possible nums1+nums2 sum? Since both x and y constraints must hold together, and queries can repeat with different thresholds, the direct per-query scan is too slow at scale, but processing everything offline in a smart order avoids repeating work.

blocks.title: Analogy: Matching Job Candidates to Two Minimum Requirements
blocks.text: Picture nums1 and nums2 as two separate skill scores for each candidate, and each query as a job needing BOTH skills above certain minimums. You want the best combined score among candidates meeting both bars, for many different jobs at once, without re-scanning every candidate for every job.

blocks.caption: Process queries from the largest x threshold down, adding candidates as their nums1 satisfies each query's x, then use a structure keyed by nums2

blocks.text: Before scanning every pair for every query, notice that sorting BOTH the array pairs and the queries by nums1/x in descending order lets a single left-to-right pass "unlock" pairs satisfying the x condition exactly once each, leaving only the y condition to handle per query, which a monotonic stack (keyed by nums2, storing the best sum) answers via binary search.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Process queries in DESCENDING order of x. As x decreases, more and more (index) pairs become "eligible" (satisfy nums1[j] >= x), and once a pair becomes eligible, it stays eligible for all remaining (smaller-x) queries.

Observation 2: This means each pair can be added to a shared structure EXACTLY ONCE, at the moment its nums1 value first satisfies the current query's x threshold, when pairs are also pre-sorted by nums1 descending.

Observation 3: Once added, only the nums2 (y) condition remains to check for each query. Maintaining the added pairs as a monotonic stack keyed by nums2 (increasing), where the SUM is also kept increasing by discarding any pair whose sum is not better than one with a smaller or equal nums2, lets a binary search quickly find the best sum among all pairs with nums2 >= the query's y.

Observation 4: The stack is monotonic in both dimensions simultaneously: since y increases going up the stack, and any pair whose sum does not exceed a later (larger-y) pair's sum is useless and discarded, the remaining sums are also increasing, making a binary search valid.

This leads to sorting pairs and queries together by nums1/x descending, adding each pair to a monotonic stack (keyed by nums2, with dominated smaller-sum entries removed) exactly once, and answering each query via a binary search on that stack for the first nums2 >= y.
For each query, scan every index directly, checking both conditions and tracking the best sum.

items: For each query [x, y], scan every index j.
If nums1[j] >= x and nums2[j] >= y, consider nums1[j]+nums2[j] as a candidate for the best sum.
Return -1 if no index satisfies both conditions.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every query independently re-scans all n indices, recomputing eligibility and the best sum from scratch.
No information is shared or reused between different queries.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times queries.length).
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the output).

Limitation: with both n and queries.length up to 10^5, this is up to 10^10 operations, far too slow; sorting both pairs and queries, then reusing a shared monotonic stack across queries, answers all of them in O((n + queries.length) log n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why per-query scanning is wasteful: the same underlying (nums1, nums2, sum) data is re-examined from scratch for every query, even though the SET of pairs satisfying a given x threshold only grows as x decreases.

The offline trick: sort both the index pairs and the queries by their x-related value in descending order. Then, walking through queries from the largest x downward, incrementally add pairs whose nums1 now satisfies the current threshold, so each pair is added exactly once across the whole process.

Handling the y condition efficiently: maintain the growing set of eligible pairs as a monotonic stack sorted by nums2 ascending, where before pushing a new pair, any existing top-of-stack entries with a sum less than or equal to the new pair's sum are popped (since a pair with a SMALLER nums2 but a smaller-or-equal sum can never be the best answer once a larger-nums2, larger-sum pair exists). This keeps both nums2 and sum simultaneously increasing up the stack.

Answering a query: binary search the monotonic stack for the first nums2 >= the query's y; because sums increase alongside nums2 in the cleaned stack, that position holds the best possible sum for that query.

Sort pairs by nums1 descending, sort queries by x descending. Walk through queries in that order, adding newly-eligible pairs into a monotonic stack (keyed by nums2, sums kept increasing by discarding dominated entries), then binary search the stack for each query's y threshold.

blocks.caption: The monotonic stack keeps nums2 and sum both increasing, enabling binary search per query

codes.python:
def maximum_sum_queries(nums1, nums2, queries):
    n = len(nums1)
    idxs = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -nums1[i])
    qn = len(queries)
    q_order = sorted(range(qn), key=lambda i: -queries[i][0])

    stack_y, stack_sum = [], []       # both strictly increasing bottom to top
    res = [-1] * qn
    ptr = 0
    for qi in q_order:
        x, y = queries[qi]
        while ptr < n and nums1[idxs[ptr]] >= x:
            i = idxs[ptr]
            yy, s = nums2[i], nums1[i] + nums2[i]
            while stack_sum and stack_sum[-1] <= s:      # remove dominated entries
                stack_sum.pop()
                stack_y.pop()
            stack_y.append(yy)
            stack_sum.append(s)
            ptr += 1
        # binary search for the first y-value >= query y
        lo, hi, best = 0, len(stack_y) - 1, -1
        while lo <= hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if stack_y[mid] >= y:
                best = stack_sum[mid]
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        res[qi] = best
    return res

blocks.text: Processing queries from the largest x downward guarantees every pair is added to the shared stack exactly once, at the correct moment. Popping dominated entries (smaller or equal sum, smaller nums2) before each push guarantees the surviving stack is simultaneously increasing in both nums2 and sum, which is exactly the condition needed for a binary search on nums2 to correctly return the maximum sum among all entries with nums2 at least the query's y.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((n + queries.length) log n), for the two sorts, plus O(log n) binary search per query and amortized O(1) per stack push/pop (each pair pushed and popped at most once).
Space: O(n + queries.length) for the sorted orders and the stack.

blocks.text: Maximum Sum Queries is a strong example of the "offline queries, sort by one dimension, sweep with a monotonic stack for the other dimension" technique, turning a two-condition maximum query into an efficient batch computation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the query has two independent threshold conditions", think: sort by one dimension to process incrementally, and use a monotonic stack or Fenwick tree for the other.

Any "answer many range/threshold queries offline" problem, solved by sorting queries and sweeping.
Monotonic stack problems like Next Greater Element, reused here to maintain a "dominance-free" set of candidates.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n times queries.length) time; the offline sort plus monotonic stack approach runs in O((n + queries.length) log n) time and O(n + queries.length) space.

items: Pattern: offline query processing, sort by one dimension (x), sweep incrementally, and use a monotonic stack for the other dimension (y).
Core Idea: add each pair to the shared stack exactly once when it becomes eligible; keep the stack simultaneously increasing in y and sum by discarding dominated entries; binary search per query.
Time: O(n times queries.length) for the brute force, O((n + queries.length) log n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: sorting both pairs and queries by the same dimension turns repeated re-scanning into a single incremental sweep.
Interview Difficulty: a hard problem combining offline sorting, a monotonic stack, and binary search in one solution.
One line memory trick: sort by x descending, sweep pairs into a dominance-free stack keyed by y, binary search per query.
